notes.written: Written 7 Nov 2026. Figures in the tables update automatically; these summaries are refreshed separately.
themes: Oil drops sharply on peace hopes

Brent fell about 13% this week to near $98 and WTI to about $90, the biggest weekly fall in months. Democrats won both houses of the US Congress in the 3 Nov midterms, which many read as limiting support for the Iran war, and Iran reportedly sent a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar. Tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz continue, so the risk has not gone away.
Two more rate rises: Australia and the UK

The RBA raised to 4.85% on 3 Nov (6–3 vote), its highest since 2008. The Bank of England raised to 4.00% on 5 Nov, its first rise since 2023; all nine members voted to raise, one for a bigger move. Both warned inflation will stay high for longer because of fuel costs.
Strong US jobs keep a December Fed rise in play

The US added 165,000 jobs in October, almost three times the forecast, and unemployment fell to 4.1%. Markets put the chance of a Fed rise on 9 Dec at roughly 75–80%. The 10-year yield is near 4.85%, about 2.6% after inflation. US inflation data on 10 Nov is the next big test.
US election weighs on the dollar, briefly
The dollar dipped after the Democratic sweep, as a split government may mean less spending, but it recovered on Friday after the jobs report. The euro is around $1.115 and the dollar about ¥157.
Inflation keeps rising outside the US
Euro-area inflation hit 4.0% in October, driven by energy (up 20.8% on a year). Swiss inflation jumped to 1.5%, a near three-year high. The Bank of England now sees UK inflation near 5% by mid-2027.

Gold bounced from a $3,875 low on 30 Oct to around $4,045, but is still about 14% lower than six months ago. Silver is near $52, down about a third in six months. A strong dollar and high real yields still weigh on both.

USD.note: Held at 3.75–4.00% on 28 Oct in a 10–2 vote; two members wanted a rise. After a strong October jobs report, markets put the chance of a rise on 9 Dec at roughly 75–80%.

EUR.note: Held on 29 Oct (deposit rate 2.50%) after two rises this year. Lagarde said a rise was discussed and did not rule one out in December; with inflation now 4.0%, markets see a December rise as likely.

GBP.note: Raised to 4.00% on 5 Nov, its first rise since 2023. Eight members voted for 4.00% and Catherine Mann for 4.25%. It expects inflation near 5% by mid-2027 and said policy is “not on a pre-set path”; the next decision is 17 Dec.

JPY.note: Held at 1.25% on 30 Oct in an 8–1 vote (one member wanted a rise). It said underlying inflation has reached its 2% target; Governor Ueda gave no firm signal this week, but December remains a real chance for the next rise.

CAD.note: Raised to 2.50% on 28 Oct, its first rise since July 2023, as oil pushes inflation up (it expects about 3.5% by year-end). Governor Macklem said more rises are likely if inflation comes in as expected or higher, but jobs are now weakening.

AUD.note: Raised to 4.85% on 3 Nov in a 6–3 vote (three wanted to hold), its fifth rise this year and highest since 2008. It said further tightening was warranted and inflation will stay above 3% through much of 2027; the next meeting is 7–8 Dec.

NZD.note: Surprised markets by holding at 2.75% on 28 Oct in a 4–3 vote (three wanted a rise). It still expects to raise later, but unemployment rose to 5.7% this week, which weakens the case for a rise on 9 Dec.

CHF.note: Held at 0% on 24 Sep and stands ready to sell francs if needed. Inflation jumped to 1.5% in October, still inside its 0–2% range; the next decision is in December.

CNY.note: Lending rates unchanged again on 20 Oct (1-year 3.00%); growth support comes mostly from the government. October surveys were mixed: the official factory index shrank, but the private Caixin index grew.

stories.USD: The jobs market came back strongly in October: employers added 165,000 jobs, nearly three times the forecast, earlier months were revised up, and unemployment fell to 4.1%. Factories and services are both growing (ISM surveys 55.5 and 54.5; above 50 means growth). Inflation is still too high (CPI 3.7% in September, PCE 3.6%), and the Fed held at 3.75–4.00% on 28 October with two members wanting a rise. Markets now see roughly a 75–80% chance of a rise on 9 December. Democrats won both houses of Congress in the 3 November midterms, which may limit government spending. The 10-year yield is near 4.85%. Next: Fed’s Waller speaks 10 Nov, CPI 10 Nov (0.3% on the month expected), Veterans Day holiday 11 Nov, jobless claims 12 Nov, PPI 13 Nov.
stories.EUR: Euro-area inflation rose to 4.0% in October, from 3.8%, the highest in three years. Energy is the main cause (up 20.8% on a year); without food and energy, inflation stayed at 2.5%. Italy hit 5.6%, while Germany eased to 2.8% thanks to a fuel tax cut. The ECB held its deposit rate at 2.50% on 29 October but Lagarde said a rise was discussed, and markets see a December rise as likely. Shoppers are pulling back: retail sales fell 0.7% in September, far worse than expected, and unemployment is 6.5%. Growth was 0.4% in Q3. Next: French holiday 11 Nov, Lagarde speaks 12 Nov (UK evening), second GDP estimate and trade 13 Nov.
stories.GBP: The Bank of England raised its rate to 4.00% on 5 November, its first rise since August 2023. All nine members voted to raise: eight for 4.00% and Catherine Mann for 4.25%. The Bank now expects inflation (3.5% in September) to climb to around 5% by mid-2027 because of energy prices, before falling back. Members were split on what comes next: some see a case for another rise, while Alan Taylor called it a “one-for-now” move. Growth has been stronger than expected, but the Bank thinks it will slow. Shoppers remain cautious (retail sales −0.4%, confidence −24). Next: Governor Bailey speaks 9 Nov, monthly and Q3 GDP 12 Nov (0.7% on the quarter expected), October inflation 18 Nov, next rate decision 17 Dec.
stories.JPY: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% on 30 October, but one member voted for a rise and the bank said underlying inflation has reached its 2% target. Governor Ueda spoke on 6 and 7 November without promising a December rise, saying it is unclear how long inflation will stay at 2%. Pay is rising fast: average earnings were up 4.6% on a year in September, well above the 3.8% expected, which supports the case for higher rates. National core inflation is 2.1% and unemployment 2.4%. But households are still cutting back (spending −3.1% on a year) and dearer energy keeps the trade balance in deficit. The yen is weak, near ¥157 per dollar. Next: household spending 9 Nov (UK 23:30), Q3 GDP 15 Nov (UK 23:50).
stories.CAD: The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.50% on 28 October, its first rise since July 2023, because high oil prices are pushing inflation up (3.1% in September). But the jobs market is weakening: employment was flat in October (−4,700), private-sector jobs fell 53,000 and unemployment rose to 6.7%, from 6.5%. Wage growth is slow at 2.2%. GDP was flat in August. The federal budget on 5 November forecast a C$62.3bn deficit this year and backs energy projects, including a new oil pipeline and LNG expansion. Exports are holding up (trade surplus C$5.4bn) and a business survey (Ivey 58.3) shows growth. Lower oil this week is a headwind for the loonie. Next: Remembrance Day holiday 11 Nov, October inflation 16 Nov.
stories.AUD: The RBA raised its rate to 4.85% on 3 November, its fifth rise this year and the highest since 2008. The vote was 6–3, with three members wanting to hold. It said inflation is “broadly based”, with rising fuel costs spreading to other prices, and will stay above its 2–3% target through much of 2027. Governor Bullock gave no promises on what comes next; most big banks expect a pause in December, though ANZ sees another rise as possible. Household spending rose a strong 0.6% in September and the trade surplus widened to A$2.8bn, but jobs fell in September (unemployment 4.7%) and house prices have fallen for seven months. Next: consumer sentiment 9 Nov (UK 23:30), NAB business survey 10 Nov (UK 00:30), inflation expectations 12 Nov, RBA meeting 7–8 Dec.
stories.NZD: The RBNZ surprised markets on 28 October by holding at 2.75% when a rise was expected; the vote was 4–3. This week’s jobs report made the case for a rise weaker: unemployment rose to 5.7% in the September quarter, from 5.6% and above the 5.5% expected, and employment fell 0.1%. Wage growth is slow (0.5% in the quarter). Inflation is 3.7% (Q3), but the RBNZ expects it to rise to about 4.4% this quarter because of fuel. The economy is weak (GDP +0.2% in Q2, trade deficit NZ$1.97bn in September). New Zealanders voted in a general election on 7 November; the official result is due 27 November. Next: few big releases before the RBNZ decision on 9 Dec.
stories.CHF: Swiss inflation jumped to 1.5% in October, from 1.0% and above the 1.3% expected, the highest since late 2023. Fuel and heating oil drove most of it; core inflation stayed low at 0.5%. That is still inside the SNB’s 0–2% target range, so the bank can keep its rate at 0%, and it stands ready to sell francs if needed. The franc is a safe haven that tends to gain when global worries rise. The economy is solid: the factory survey rose to 56.7 (above 50 means growth) and unemployment is low at 3.1%, though retail sales growth slowed to 1.6% on a year. Next: no big Swiss releases on the calendar in the coming week; the next SNB decision is in December.
stories.CNY: China is shown because it drives AUD, NZD and commodity demand. Growth was 4.5% on a year in Q3, meeting the 4.5–5% target thanks mostly to exports (trade surplus $133.5bn in September). October surveys were mixed: the official factory index fell to 49.3 (below 50 means shrinking) as export orders dropped, but the private Caixin index, which covers more smaller and export firms, held at 52.0. Factories keep cutting prices because of fierce competition. Demand at home is soft (retail sales +1.1%) as the property slump continues, inflation is low (0.9%) and lending rates were left at 3.00%. Next: October inflation 9 Nov (0.8% expected), October trade 10 Nov (surplus $126.5bn expected).

oil.title: Oil (WTI and Brent)
oil.what: The price of crude oil. Brent is the global benchmark, WTI the US one.
oil.now: Brent fell about 13% this week to near $98 and WTI to about $90, the steepest weekly drop in months. That is below early-May levels (about $106–116), but still about a third above the late-June low near $72. Democrats winning the US Congress raised hopes of a quicker end to the Iran war, Iran reportedly sent a nuclear proposal through Qatar, and Gulf exports have recovered close to pre-war levels. Attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz continue, and any breakdown in talks could push prices back up.
oil.links: High oil helps oil exporters (CAD) and hurts importers (JPY, EUR). It feeds straight into inflation, which is why central banks have turned to raising rates.

gold.title: Gold
gold.what: Gold priced in US dollars. It pays no interest, so it competes with what investors can earn elsewhere.
gold.now: Around $4,045, about 14% lower than six months ago and about 27% below January’s peak near $5,500. It bounced about 4% this week from a $3,875 low on 30 Oct, but slipped on Friday after strong US jobs data lifted the dollar and yields. High real interest rates (US 10-year after inflation about 2.6%) and bets on a December Fed rise are the headwind; central-bank buying and safe-haven demand are the support.
gold.links: Gold tends to rise when real yields fall, the dollar weakens or fear spikes. It often moves with CHF and JPY as a safe haven, and with AUD, since Australia is a big producer.

silver.title: Silver
silver.what: Half precious metal, half industrial metal (solar panels, electronics), so it swings more than gold.
silver.now: Around $52, down about a third in six months (from about $79 in early May), a much bigger fall than gold’s. It faces the same rate headwind plus worries about factory demand (China’s official factory index fell below 50 in October).
silver.links: Follows gold in direction but with bigger swings; weaker Chinese industry weighs on it.
